paragraphs.heading: Free modules
paragraphs.text: A module is called free when it has a basis, which is a generating set that is linearly independent. Every vector space is a free module. But when the ring of coefficients is not a division ring, which in the commutative case means not a field, some modules are not free.

paragraphs.heading: Building one from any set
paragraphs.text: Starting from any set S and any ring R, one can form a free R-module whose basis is S. It is called the free module on S, and its elements are formal R-linear combinations of the members of S. A free abelian group is exactly a free module over the ring Z of integers.

paragraphs.heading: Rank
paragraphs.text: If R has invariant basis number, then any two bases of a free module have the same cardinality, or size. Nonzero commutative rings, for example, have this property. The cardinality of a basis is called the rank of the free module. When it is finite, the module is free of finite rank, or free of rank n when the rank is known to be n.

paragraphs.heading: Examples
paragraphs.text: Over itself, any ring R is a free module of rank one, and any unit element serves as a basis. For a non-negative integer n, the product Rⁿ of n copies of R is free, and its rank is n when R has invariant basis number. If R is commutative, the polynomial ring R[X] is free, with a possible basis 1, X, X², and so on. Over a principal ideal domain such as Z, every submodule of a free module is free.

paragraphs.heading: Sums, products and surprises
paragraphs.text: A direct sum of free modules is free. An infinite cartesian product of free modules, by contrast, is generally not free. Sometimes whether a module is free cannot be settled at all in the set-theoretic sense. A famous case is the Whitehead problem: is a Whitehead group free? The question turns out to be independent of ZFC.

paragraphs.heading: Wider classes of modules
paragraphs.text: Many results that hold for free modules carry over to larger classes. Projective modules are direct summands of free modules. Flat modules are those where tensoring with them keeps exact sequences exact, and torsion-free modules form a broader class still. Kaplansky's theorem says a projective module over a local ring, even a non-commutative one, is free. For a finitely generated module over a principal ideal domain such as Z, being free, projective, flat and torsion-free all mean the same thing.
